newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Sievert sees no early Bundesbank rate rise.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Sievert sees no early Bundesbank rate rise.

text.p: The German Bundesbank will have no grounds to raise interest rates any time soon and may even have scope to lower credit costs further this economic cycle, a member of the bank's policy-making council said on Tuesday.

Olaf Sievert, president of the regional central bank based in the east German city of Leipzig, also said in a speech he believed worries that currency markets could be very turbulent in the run-up to European monetary union were exaggerated.
Speaking at a reception in Leipzig, Sievert said: "I see nothing which could give us grounds to take a firmer grip on the monetary reins."

He added that it was hard to say whether there could be scope for further cuts in leading interest rates this cycle. The Bundesbank has held its Lombard and discount rates steady since April but it reduced a key money market rate in August.
"Whether there is room to manoeuvre on the downside remains to be seen," he said, according to the text of his speech which was released in advance.

Sievert said the outlook for German inflation continued to be favourable despite increases in raw materials prices. "The prospects for the future also look good," he said, noting annual German inflation is now running at around 1.4 percent.

This fact, together with expectations that money supply growth will slow in 1997, meant that the Bundesbank did not have to be too concerned about the fact that M3 money supply growth overshot the central bank's target in 1996, he said.
"The overshooting of the goal is no reason for considerable concern, given that the pace of money supply growth had already started to slow last spring," he said.
Good news for the economy lay in the fact that the excessive appreciation in the mark seen in 1995, when the dollar tumbled to an all-time low, had corrected.
"The appreciation of the mark seen in spring 1995, which was absolutely unfitting for the real economy, has in the meantime been corrected," Sievert said.

The likelihood of further currency market turbulence ahead of the planned creation of the euro in 1999 also seemed smaller than many feared, he said, adding that he did not expect this to be a major problem over the next two years.

Looking ahead to possible problems, Sievert said: "I am not thinking here so much of the widespread fear that speculative trends on financial markets could create turbulence which will make the task of monetary policy more difficult."
"There are possibbly exaggerated worries here," he added.

Growing consensus in financial markets that European Monetary Union (EMU) would start on time in 1999 meant that any speculation was more likely to be "stabilising speculation, and not destabilising speculation".
"That is, in any case, true for the internal relationship between the currency areas which will form a single currency area from the start of monetary union," Sievert added.
He added that it would be more difficult to ensure stable relationships between currencies which entered EMU and those initially left outside.
Countries which wish to merge their currencies in the euro from 1999 onward must meet goals on public deficits, public debt, interest rates, exchange rates and inflation this year.
In his text, Sievert also dismissed a French proposal to create a "stability council" as a political counterweight to the future European Central Bank.
This proposal appeared to be a meaningless attempt to find some form of mediator for monetary policy, which had the clearly defined role of price stability as its absolute priority.
Noting that the council, in contrast to the ECB itself, would have no real decision-making power, he added, "But why then bother with such a council at all?"
